name: Warehouse Ops Manager - Moderately Misaligned - SwiftHaul
description: Warehouse Operations Manager at SwiftHaul Logistics during a 40% volume growth year. Employee sees themselves as the reason the operation held together (throughput, put-away process, client relationships). Manager acknowledges those strengths but sees material cost in safety incidents, two supervisor resignations, 60% overtime overrun, and two missed client SLAs. Primary disagreement: people management and team leadership. Secondary: safety compliance trending down while throughput went up.

answers.employee: During this review period I was the Warehouse Operations Manager for SwiftHaul's main fulfillment site, which is what I've been for the last three years. My core responsibilities are running the day-to-day operation, hitting throughput targets, managing the shift supervisors and floor staff, keeping the two large e-commerce client accounts happy, and owning the operating budget for the warehouse. This year my scope expanded pretty significantly because we brought on two major e-commerce clients and volume went up around 40 percent year over year, without any headcount increase approved. That expansion wasn't a temporary project — it became the new baseline for the operation, and I think that's the single most important piece of context for how my performance should be evaluated. The expectation on paper stayed the same, which was to keep the site running smoothly, but in practice the bar moved up a lot and nobody adjusted the scorecard for it. I want that to be on the table when we talk about results.
answers.manager: The employee has been the Warehouse Operations Manager for the SwiftHaul main fulfillment site for three years and continued in that role through this review period. Their core responsibilities are throughput and SLA performance for the site, managing the shift supervisors and floor staff, safety and compliance on the floor, and operating budget ownership. Their scope did materially expand this year with the two new e-commerce clients and the roughly 40 percent volume increase, and that expansion should absolutely be considered when evaluating results. It is fair to say the scorecard on paper did not fully catch up to the new volume. At the same time, safety, people management, and budget are core responsibilities of this role and did not go away because volume grew — those are still part of what the employee owns and should be evaluated against.

answers.employee: The goals that mattered most this year were, first, holding throughput through the volume spike so we didn't miss on the two new client accounts, and second, getting the new put-away process launched so we could reduce pick errors. Those were the ones I focused on because those were the ones the business was going to feel immediately. Safety and overtime were also on the sheet but honestly, when you have volume up 40 percent and the same headcount, something has to give — and I made the call to protect throughput and client delivery first. I think that call was communicated pretty clearly to my director in our one-on-ones. The success measure people care about most is on-time to client, and that was what I optimized for.
answers.manager: The employee is right that throughput and the put-away improvement were priorities this year, and both of those were communicated clearly. Where the employee's view diverges from mine is on what else was on the goal sheet. Safety incident rate, supervisor retention, overtime budget adherence, and client SLA attainment were all explicit goals for this role at the start of the year, not optional trade-offs. The volume growth is a legitimate constraint, but the trade-off framing the employee is describing — that something had to give — was not authorized and was not discussed with me at the time. If it had been raised as a goal conflict earlier, we could have talked about pulling in temp labor or renegotiating SLAs. That conversation did not happen.

answers.employee: The results this year speak for themselves. We processed 40 percent more volume with the same headcount, which is a big deal. The put-away process I rolled out in Q2 cut our pick error rate by around 18 percent, which our biggest client specifically called out in a QBR. I personally covered floor supervisor shifts on more than a dozen nights during peak to keep the operation moving when we were short-staffed. Both new client accounts are still with us and still active, and I've built strong relationships with their operations leads. Yes, we missed a couple of SLA windows late in the year, but in context — 40 percent more volume, same team — I think the overall result was strong. Not many people could have held it together the way I did.
answers.manager: The employee delivered real, measurable wins this year that deserve credit. Throughput held through the volume growth, the put-away process is genuinely working and the 18 percent pick error reduction is verified in the client QBR, and their relationships with both new client operations leads are strong. Those are meaningful outcomes. The picture is more mixed on the other side. Two client SLAs were missed in Q3 — those are contractual and they will factor into next year's renewal conversation. OSHA-recordable safety incidents at the site trended up year over year. Two shift supervisors resigned in the past six months, and the exit interviews both cited communication style with the employee as a factor. Overtime came in about 60 percent over budget. So the accomplishments are real, and the costs of getting there are also real and need to be weighed in the evaluation.

answers.employee: On execution, I think I've been extremely reliable this year. When supervisors quit or called out, I stepped in personally to run the floor. When the put-away process needed to be redesigned, I owned that end to end without asking for outside help. I don't miss commitments, and when something is at risk I'm on it before it becomes a problem. The two SLA misses in Q3 were driven by an inbound-receiving bottleneck on the vendor side that was outside my control — I escalated it as soon as I saw it. If there's a fair critique here it's that I've been running hot and taking too much on personally, but I'd rather do that than let the site slip.
answers.manager: The employee's willingness to step in personally is a real strength and I don't want to take that away from them. Where I see execution risk is exactly in the pattern of personally covering rather than solving the underlying capacity and staffing problem. That approach masked how thin the team actually was, and I only found out how bad it was when the second supervisor resigned. On the Q3 SLA misses, the vendor-side receiving issue was real, but the escalation to me came late — after we had already missed the first window. Earlier escalation would have let us renegotiate with the client before we defaulted. So the ownership piece is strong on the individual level and uneven on the systems level — building a reliable team, escalating early, and not absorbing everything personally are all part of this role.

answers.employee: Quality-wise, I'm proud of the work. The put-away redesign was careful, well thought out, and it's holding up. Pick accuracy is up. Client-facing communication has been professional. I'll be honest that safety documentation slipped a bit toward the back half of the year — logs weren't always current, some near-miss reports were late. That's a paperwork issue born out of everyone being maxed out, not a real safety problem on the floor. The actual operation is running clean.
answers.manager: The put-away process is high-quality work and the pick accuracy improvement is verifiable. That part deserves recognition. On safety, I have to push back on the framing. It is not just paperwork. OSHA-recordable incidents at the site are up year over year — that is on-the-floor reality, not documentation. The near-miss reports being late matters because near-miss data is how you prevent the next recordable incident, and we lost that visibility for months. In a warehouse role, safety compliance is a quality standard, not an administrative task, and treating it as paperwork is where I most disagree with the employee's self-assessment.

answers.employee: Communication with my director has been open and regular — we do a standing one-on-one and I flag issues as they come up. Client communication is a strength of mine and both new clients have said so directly. With the floor team, I run a tight ship. I'm direct, I set clear expectations, and I hold people to them. I know a couple of supervisors left and I'm sure they had things to say on the way out, but honestly the ones who stayed are performing well and the ones who left weren't the right fit for a high-volume operation. I don't think that's a communication problem, that's a fit problem.
answers.manager: Client communication and the standing one-on-one cadence with me are both real strengths. Where the employee and I most sharply disagree is on the internal team side. Two shift supervisors resigned in the last six months. In both exit interviews, the same theme came up — the employee's communication style is described as short, aggressive under pressure, and dismissive of pushback. That is a consistent signal from two independent sources and it needs to be taken seriously rather than reframed as a fit problem. The floor staff also raised concerns in the last engagement survey about how issues are received when they're brought up. I don't think this is a character issue — I think it is a leadership skill gap that shows up under sustained pressure, and it is the single biggest thing I want to work on with the employee next period.

answers.employee: On growth, I've stretched a lot this year. I've handled a 40 percent volume increase, redesigned a core process, and kept two demanding clients happy. I feel ready for more scope — a multi-site role or a regional operations role would be a good next step. The development area I'd point to is that I probably need to get better at delegating and building bench strength on the supervisor level so I'm not the single point of failure. That's a real gap and I own it.
answers.manager: The self-awareness on delegation and bench strength is genuinely good and I want to build on that. That is exactly the right area to work on. My assessment on readiness for expanded scope is that we're not there yet, and I want to be honest about why. Multi-site leadership requires being able to run through people rather than personally, and this year showed that under pressure the employee defaults to doing it themselves and to a communication style that is losing us supervisors. Those are exactly the things that scale poorly. I want to see one full year of stable supervisor retention, safety trending back down, and the employee visibly building the team before we open the readiness conversation. In terms of support, I'd like to put them into a people-leadership coaching program next quarter and pair them with a mentor from another region.

answers.employee: The single biggest context factor is the 40 percent volume increase with no approved headcount. That has to be central to any fair evaluation. Second, the inbound-receiving vendor issue in Q3 was outside my control and it was the primary driver of the SLA misses. Third, the peers I get compared to are running sites at flat volume — that isn't a like-for-like comparison. For next period, the things I'd want clarified are headcount authorization to match volume, a real overtime budget that reflects reality, and clearer escalation paths on vendor issues so I'm not carrying that alone. With those in place, I'm confident I can deliver a cleaner year on safety and turnover too.
answers.manager: I fully agree that the 40 percent volume increase with no headcount adjustment is a real and material context factor and it will be weighted in the evaluation. The Q3 vendor receiving issue is also real, though the late escalation is on the employee. The peer-comparison point is fair — this site is not a flat-volume site and the evaluation should reflect that. For next period, the things I want on the record are: I will support a headcount request and a realistic overtime budget going into peak, and in exchange I need explicit ownership of supervisor retention with a target, safety incident rate back to or below prior baseline, earlier escalation on cross-functional risks — inside the first week, not the first month — and demonstrated investment in coaching and developing the supervisor bench. If we agree on those as the success measures for next period, this becomes a clear, fair evaluation and a clear plan.
